title: Kavanah, intention
hookLine: Jewish prayer asks for kavanah, the heart aimed at what the lips are saying

cards: Before they prayed, the pious ones of old would wait an hour. That's how the Mishnah, the collection of early Jewish law, describes them. Not to get the words ready.
They knew the words. They waited to get the heart ready, to direct it toward their Father in heaven. Then the same passage turns strict.
Once you've begun, even if a king greets you, don't answer him. Even if a snake is wound around your heel, don't stop. That's a great deal of attention for a few minutes of words.

teach.b: The name for what they waited for is kavanah, usually translated intention, or directed intention: the heart aimed, the way you aim your steps down a road.
The Mishnah uses this language of aiming; in one rule about reciting the Shema, the question is simply whether a person directed his heart. The roots reach into the Torah.
Deuteronomy, in the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation, asks Israel "to serve Him with all your heart and with all your soul."
The rabbis of the Talmud asked a sharp question about that line: what kind of service happens in the heart? Their answer was prayer.

teach.h: PRAYER, THE SERVICE OF THE HEART.
teach.b: So prayer is the service of the heart, and kavanah is what makes it the heart's. Then a tension Jewish teachers have turned over for a long time.
Jewish prayer has fixed words, said at fixed times. The fixed part has its own name, keva. Kavanah is the living part.
Lean only on keva and the words run on autopilot. Wait only for kavanah and you might never get around to praying.
The Mishnah names the danger in one line: whoever makes their prayer a fixed task, their prayer is not a plea.

teach.h: TO SERVE HIM WITH ALL YOUR HEART.
teach.b: Yet the tradition doesn't throw out the fixed words because the heart wanders. It keeps the words, and keeps asking for the aim.
And the idea reaches past prayer: Jewish teachers speak of kavanah in eating, in giving, in the small commanded acts of an ordinary day.

how: Jews who pray the set daily prayers try to bring kavanah, directed intention, to the fixed words; teachers in the tradition also speak of bringing it to blessings, meals and other daily acts.

o: the fixed words said at set prayer times
a quiet hour of waiting before you pray
the heart aimed at what you're doing or saying

s: kavanah means throwing out the fixed words of prayer
the tradition keeps the fixed words, keva, and asks for the aim of the heart inside them.
the Mishnah says not to stop praying even for a snake around your heel
even if a king greets you, don't answer; even if a snake is wound around your heel, don't stop.
the rabbis read "serve Him with all your heart" as being about prayer
they asked what service happens in the heart, and answered: prayer.

games.q: you're in the middle of the fixed prayer. a king walks up and greets you. what does the Mishnah say to do?
o: answer him politely, then go back to praying.
stop, and start the whole prayer over.
games.why: the Mishnah says even a king's greeting shouldn't break the prayer, and not even a snake at your heel. that's how seriously it takes the aim of the heart.

practice: Pick one small act you can do right now: a sip of water, folding your hands, standing up from your chair.
Before you do it, wait one breath, the way the pious ones waited, and know what you're about to do and why; if you pray, point it toward God, and if you don't, toward the person or the day it serves.
Then do it slowly, all the way through, and nothing else.

wordCard.voice: Kavanah. Directed intention: the heart aimed at what the lips or hands are doing, in Jewish prayer and beyond it. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: intention, the heart directed toward what you are doing.

carryVoice: Your line: kavanah. The same act can be done with the heart pointed at it, or on the way to something else. Back tomorrow, same hill.
